verses.translation: And it came to pass{H1961}, when Yeshua{H3442} finished{H3615} these{H428} words{H1697}, he passed{H5674} from the Galil{H1551} and came{H935} to the ends{H7098} of the land{H776} of Yehudah{H3063} which is beyond{H5676} the Yarden{H3383}.

one_way_hebrew: ויהי כאשר כלה... הדברים האלה — the Torah's own closing formula (ויהי ככלות משה לדבר את כל הדברים האלה, Deut 32:45): each discourse of this gospel closes as Moses' discourses close. Greek καὶ ἐγένετο ὅτε ἐτέλεσεν is a calque of exactly this.
בעבר הירדן — 'beyond the Yarden': the Torah's fixed regional name (Gen 50:10-11; Deut 1:1).
textual_notes: Shem Tov's own section heading פרק פ״א (Perek 81) begins here.

verses.translation: And the Pharisees approached{H5066} him to test him{H5254}, and they asked him{H7592}, saying{H559}: Is it permitted{H5425} to leave{H5800} one's wife{H802} for any matter{H6045}, and to give{H5414} her a get?

one_way_hebrew: מותר — 'is it PERMITTED': the question is asked in the halakhic form (muttar, from the same נתר of the loosing-grants at 16:19; 18:18) — a she'elah put to a posek. Greek ἔξεστιν translates the court-word.

גט — the get, the rabbinic name of the divorce document itself (a thousand pages of tractate Gittin); Greek Matthew has no noun here at all ('to put away his wife for every cause'). The Hebrew asks about the actual instrument of Jewish law.

בשום עניין — 'for ANY matter': the very formula of the Hillel-Shammai dispute (m. Gittin 9:10 — Beit Hillel permitted divorce 'even if she burned his dish,' on Deut 24:1's ערות דבר). The Hebrew question is the first-century question in its own terms.

verses.translation: And he answered{H6030} them: Have you not read{H7121} of their Maker{H6213} — that of old{H6924}, male{H2145} and female{H5347} He created them{H1254}?

one_way_hebrew: זכר ונקבה בראם — Gen 1:27 and 5:2 in their own consonants; the Hebrew answer simply IS the verse. And לעושיהם — 'their MAKER' — is the Tanakh's epithet (Job 35:10, אלוה עשי; Ps 149:2; Isa 54:5, כי בעליך עשיך — 'your Maker is your husband,' the marriage-text itself). Greek ὁ κτίσας ('the one who created') flattens the title.
textual_notes: Howard's apparatus (19:4): לעושיהם] שעושיהם ABDEFG.

verses.translation: And he said{H559}: Therefore{H3651} shall a man{H376} leave{H5800} his father{H1} and his mother{H517}, and cleave{H1692} to his wife{H802}, and they shall be one{H259} flesh{H1320}.

one_way_hebrew: Gen 2:24 verbatim (על כן יעזב איש את אביו ואת אמו ודבק באשתו) — quoted without a seam, in the Torah's own words, where the Greek must translate them.
textual_notes: Howard's apparatus (19:5): איש] האדם G.

verses.translation: If so, they are not two{H8147} but one{H259} flesh{H1320}; and what the Creator{H1254} has joined{H2266}, no man{H120} is able{H3201} to separate{H6504}.

one_way_hebrew: הבורא — 'the CREATOR' (the borei, from Gen 1:1's ברא just quoted in v. 4's בראם): the Hebrew keeps the creation-verb running through the argument. Greek has generic ὁ θεός ('God').
שחבר... להפריד — joined (חבר) against separated (פרד): the same verb-pair this text uses of the eagles joining (24:28) and the wicked separated out (24:51); marriage is a chibbur no man may undo.
textual_notes: Howard's apparatus (19:6): no variants recorded.

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to him: If so{H3651}, why{H4069} did Moshe{H4872} command{H6680} to give{H5414} a get of divorcement{H3748} and send her{H7971} from his house{H1004}?

one_way_hebrew: כריתות... ושלחה מביתו — Deut 24:1's own words (ספר כריתת... ושלחה מביתו): the challenge is mounted in the Torah's exact vocabulary, with the living word גט set beside Deuteronomy's כריתות — the medieval court term and the Torah term side by side, exactly as a Hebrew jurist speaks.
textual_notes: Howard's apparatus (19:7): ויאמר] ויאמרו G; לתת] + לה ABDEFG; ושלחה] ולשלח A.

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to them: For the crookedness{H6143} of the mouth{H6310} of your heart{H3824}, Moshe{H4872} told{H559} you to leave{H5800} your wives{H802} — but from everlasting{H5769} it was not so{H3651}.

one_way_hebrew: לעקשות פה לבבכם — 'for the crookedness of the mouth of your heart': Prov 4:24's עקשות פה ('crooked speech') driven inward to the heart (cf. Prov 17:20, עקש לב). Greek σκληροκαρδία ('hard-heartedness') is one flat word; the Hebrew diagnoses a heart whose speech is twisted — the false grounds men plead for divorce.
ומעולם לא היה כן — 'from EVERLASTING it was not so' (מעולם): Greek has 'from the beginning (ἀπ' ἀρχῆς) it was not so'; the Hebrew word reaches behind time's beginning to the standing order of things.

verses.translation: I say{H559} to you: everyone{H3605} who leaves{H5800} his wife{H802} and takes{H3947} another{H312} — if not on account of adultery{H5004} — commits adultery{H5003}; and he who takes the divorced woman{H1644} commits adultery{H5003}.

one_way_hebrew: The whole ruling runs on the Torah's own roots: נאף (the seventh commandment's verb, Exod 20:13 — quoted below at v. 18) and גרושה (the divorced woman of Lev 21:7,14; 22:13). The exception is ניאוף — the thing the commandment itself names — where Greek has πορνεία, a broader word that has bred centuries of debate; in the Hebrew the exception and the sin are the same root, tight as a legal clause should be.

verses.translation: And his disciples{H8527} said{H559} to him: If so is the matter{H1697} of a man{H120} with his wife{H802}, it is not good{H2896} to take{H3947} her.

one_way_hebrew: לא טוב — the disciples answer Gen 2:18 backwards: where the Maker said לא טוב היות האדם לבדו ('it is NOT GOOD for the man to be alone'), they conclude it is not good to take a wife at all — and the next verses correct them. The exchange only rhymes in Hebrew, where לא טוב is Genesis' own verdict-formula.

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to them: This{H2088} word{H1697} is not for everyone{H3605}, but for him to whom{H4310} it is given{H5414}.

textual_notes: No variants recorded in Howard's apparatus for this verse. The printed text carries a stray vowel-point before אלא; points are stripped here.

verses.translation: For there are{H3426} eunuchs{H5631} from their birth{H8435} — these are they who have not sinned{H2398}; and there are eunuchs{H5631} of their own doing{H6106}, who subdue{H3533} their inclination{H3336} for the sake of the kingdom{H4438} of heaven{H8064} — these are wise ones{H2450} of great{H1419} degree{H4609}. Whoever{H4310} is able{H3201} to understand{H995}, let him understand{H995}.

one_way_hebrew: שכובשים את יצרם — 'who SUBDUE THEIR YETZER': the rabbinic definition of the mighty man word for word — 'who is strong? he who subdues his yetzer' (הכובש את יצרו, m. Avot 4:1) — with יצר itself from Gen 6:5; 8:21 (יצר לב האדם). Where Greek Matthew has 'made themselves eunuchs (εὐνούχισαν ἑαυτούς) for the kingdom,' a sentence that sent Origen to the knife, the Hebrew says continence, not castration: they master the inclination. The difference is not stylistic — it is the difference between a Greek reader's mutilation and a Hebrew reader's middah.
מי שיוכל להבין יבין — the mashal-closer in its native form (cf. Dan 12:10, והמשכלים יבינו).
greek_deviations: The base text has TWO classes of eunuchs, not three: born eunuchs ('who have not sinned') and self-mastering ones. The middle class of the Greek — 'eunuchs made eunuchs by men' — is absent; mss ABDEFG supply ויש סריסים עשויים בידי אדם, assimilating to the Greek (the Vat. Ebr. 100 Hebrew Matthew has the three-class form).

Of the born eunuchs the Hebrew says אלו הם אשר לא חטאו — 'these are they who have NOT SINNED' — answering a standing question (cf. John 9:2, 'who sinned, this man or his parents?') that the Greek text never raises.
translation_notes: מתולדותם — so the scan (from תולדות, 'generations, birth'); the circulating transcription's מתולכותם is a typo, corrected here.

verses.translation: Then{H227} children{H3206} were brought{H935} to him, that he might lay{H7760} his hand{H3027} on them and pray{H6419} over them; but his disciples{H8527} were driving them away{H1644}.

In Hebrew the irony is audible — fresh from the divorce dispute, the disciples try to divorce the children from the master; Greek ἐπετίμησαν ('rebuked') has no echo.

verses.translation: And one{H259} young man{H970} approached{H5066} him, bowing{H7812} to him, and said{H559} to him: Rabbi, what{H335} good{H2896} shall I do{H6213} to acquire{H7069} the life{H2416} of the world to come?

one_way_hebrew: לקנות חיי העה״ב — 'to ACQUIRE the life of THE WORLD TO COME': the question is asked in the rabbis' own terms — koneh chayyei ha-olam ha-ba (m. Avot 2:7, 'one who has acquired words of Torah has acquired the life of the world to come'), with the ms abbreviation העה״ב as at 16:25-26. Greek has 'that I may have eternal life (ζωὴν αἰώνιον)'; the Hebrew has the acquisition-idiom of the study-house.
ר׳ — the ms writes the standing abbreviation for 'Rabbi'; Greek διδάσκαλε ('teacher') translates the title.

verses.translation: And he answered{H6030} him: Why{H4100} do you ask{H7592} about good{H2896}? Man{H120} is not good{H2896}, for El{H410} alone{H905} is good. And if you desire{H7521} to enter{H935} into life{H2416}, keep{H8104} the commandments{H4687}.

greek_deviations: אין האדם טוב כי האל לבדו הוא טוב — 'MAN is not good, for El alone is good.' The Greek texts split over this verse ('why do you ask me about the good?' / 'why do you call me good? none is good but God'), and the old objection built on the Greek — that Yeshua distances himself from goodness — has no footing in the Hebrew: the sentence contrasts האדם (man as such) with האל, not the speaker with God. It is Ps 14:2-3's verdict (אין עשה טוב) in one clause.
שמור המצוות — 'KEEP the commandments' (שמר, the Torah's own guarding-verb, Deut 5:29): the way into life is the mitzvot, stated without embarrassment.
translation_notes: ואם — the scan reads ואם; the circulating transcription's ואמ (non-final mem) is a typo, corrected here.

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to him: Which{H4100} are they? And Yeshua{H3442} said to him: You shall not murder{H7523}; you shall not steal{H1589}; you shall not answer{H6030} against your neighbor{H7453} as a false{H8267} witness{H5707}.

one_way_hebrew: The commandments come in the consonants of Exod 20:13-16 / Deut 5:17-20 themselves — לא תרצח, לא תגנוב, לא תענה ברעך עד שקר — the text does not translate the Decalogue, it recites it.
greek_deviations: The list lacks לא תנאף ('you shall not commit adultery') — an eye-skip between the identical לא ת... openings, of the same mechanical kind as the haplographies Howard logs across chapter 18; only ms D supplies it. That the omission is scribal, not editorial, is shown by v. 9 above, where the text has just legislated against ניאוף by name.

verses.translation: Honor{H3513} your father{H1} and your mother{H517}; and you shall love{H157} your neighbor{H7453} as yourself{H3644}.

one_way_hebrew: כבד את אביך ואת אמך (Exod 20:12) and ואהבת לרעך כמוך (Lev 19:18) — both verbatim, the second with Leviticus' own ל before רעך, a construction Greek cannot carry (ἀγαπήσεις τὸν πλησίον σου). The pairing of Decalogue with Lev 19:18 as its summary is itself a Hebrew habit of thought (cf. 22:39).

verses.translation: And the young man{H970} said{H559} to him: All{H3605} these{H428} I have kept{H8104}; and what{H4100} do I still{H5750} lack{H2637}?

one_way_hebrew: ומה יחסר לי — 'what do I LACK?' (חסר): the shepherd-psalm's verb (Ps 23:1, לא אחסר) and Deut 2:7 ('you have lacked nothing'). The rich young man's question is the psalm's negation.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} said{H559} to him: If you desire{H7521} to be whole{H8535}, go{H1980} and sell{H4376} all{H3605} that is yours and give it{H5414} to the poor{H6041}, and there will be for you a treasure{H214} in heaven{H8064}; and come{H935} after{H310} me.

one_way_hebrew: תם (H8535) — 'whole, blameless': Job's word (איש תם וישר, Job 1:1,8) and Jacob's (איש תם, Gen 25:27). Greek τέλειος ('perfect') is a philosophical measure; תם is a covenant character — undivided. The man who kept all and lacks one thing is being offered Job's adjective.
עניים (H6041) — the Torah's poor, to whom giving is command (Deut 15:11); אוצר בשמים — the treasury relocated (cf. Deut 28:12, YHWH's own אוצר in heaven).
textual_notes: Howard's apparatus (19:21): אליו] לו EFG; ויהיה] ויהי A; ובא] ולך G.

verses.translation: And it came to pass{H1961}, when the young man{H970} heard{H8085}, he went off{H1980}, because he did not have many{H7227} landholdings.

greek_deviations: The base text reads the OPPOSITE of the Greek: 'he went off because he did NOT have many landholdings' — where Greek Matthew has 'he went away sorrowful, for he HAD many possessions.' Ms A reads שהיו לו ('because he HAD'), matching the Greek, and mss ABDEF add זעף ('he went off ANGRY/dejected'). Either the base scribe intruded שלא, or the base preserves a sharper irony: the man who would not sell what he had is described as one who had nothing that mattered. The translation renders the text as printed; Howard's English does the same.
translation_notes: קרקעות — karka'ot, 'landed properties': the rabbinic law-word for real estate (the karka of countless mishnayot), where Greek has κτήματα ('possessions'). The teller's own property-law vocabulary again.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} said{H559} to his disciples{H8527}: Amen{H543}, I say{H559} to you that it is hard{H3515} for the rich man{H6223} to enter{H935} the kingdom{H4438} of heaven{H8064}.

one_way_hebrew: כבד — 'HEAVY': in Hebrew the rich man's difficulty is told in the weight-word (כבד) that is also the wealth-word (Gen 13:2, ואברם כבד מאד במקנה — 'Abram was very HEAVY in cattle'). The rich man is too heavy for the narrow way; Greek δυσκόλως ('with difficulty') has no scales in it.
textual_notes: No variants recorded in Howard's apparatus for this verse.

verses.translation: And again{H5750} I say{H559} to you: it is easier{H7031} for the camel{H1581} to pass{H935} through the eye{H5869} of the needle than for the rich man{H6223} into the kingdom{H4438} of heaven{H8064}.

one_way_hebrew: בעין המחט — 'the EYE of the needle': the Hebrew idiom exactly as the Talmud speaks it (b. Berakhot 55b, 'they do not show a man a golden palm or an elephant passing through the eye of a needle,' קופא דמחטא), with מחט the rabbinic needle-word. The saying lives in the same proverb-world as the rabbis' impossible-passings; Greek τρύπημα ('hole') is anatomically blind — only Hebrew calls it an eye.
textual_notes: No variants recorded in Howard's apparatus for this verse.

verses.translation: And the disciples{H8527} heard{H8085} and were greatly{H3966} astonished{H8539}, and said{H559} to Yeshua{H3442}: If so, who{H4310} can{H3201} save{H3467}?

one_way_hebrew: ויתמהו — the astonishment-verb of Gen 43:33 and Hab 1:5 (התמהו תמהו); and the question is asked with the yasha-root again (להושיע), the root of the Savior's own name, as at 24:13 and 16:25.

verses.translation: And he turned{H6437} to them and said{H559}: Before{H5048} the sons{H1121} of man{H120} the thing{H1697} is hard{H7186}, but before Elohim{H430} everything{H3605} is easy{H7031} to be.

one_way_hebrew: The answer stands on Gen 18:14 (היפלא מיהוה דבר — 'is any THING too hard for YHWH?') and Jer 32:17 (לא יפלא ממך כל דבר) — the Hebrew keeps דבר from the question in the answer, as those texts do. Greek has 'with men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible' — power-language; the Hebrew's קשה/קל is weight-language, finishing v. 23's scales: what is heavy before men is light before Elohim.
textual_notes: אלקים — the ms uses the reverent ק-spelling, as throughout.
Howard's apparatus (19:26): הדבר] הכל דבר G; האלקים] האלים A.

verses.translation: And Petros answered{H6030} and said{H559} to him: Behold{H2009}, we have left{H5800} everything{H3605} to go{H1980} after you{H310}; what{H4100} will there be for us?

one_way_hebrew: עזבנו — Petros claims with the same verb the chapter has been turning over: the man leaves father and mother (v. 5), the husband leaves his wife (v. 9), the rich man will not leave his goods (v. 22), and the disciples have left everything (vv. 27, 29). One Hebrew root (עזב) carries the whole argument; the Greek scatters it across ἀφίημι and καταλείπω.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} said{H559}: Amen{H543}, I say{H559} to you who go{H1980} after me{H310}: on the day{H3117} of the judgment{H1779}, when the Man{H120} sits{H3427} on the throne{H3678} of his glory{H3519}, you also shall sit{H3427} on twelve thrones{H3678} — the twelve{H8147} tribes{H7626} of Yisrael{H3478}.

one_way_hebrew: כסא כבודו — 'the throne of his glory': Jer 14:21's phrase (כסא כבודך) and 1 Sam 2:8 (כסא כבוד ינחלם — Hannah's song, where the needy inherit it); the enthronement promise is built from those texts.
greek_deviations: ביום הדין — 'on the DAY OF JUDGMENT': the Hebrew has yom ha-din, Israel's own name for the great assize, where Greek Matthew has ἐν τῇ παλιγγενεσίᾳ — 'in the regeneration,' a Stoic technical term found nowhere else in the gospels. One text speaks the synagogue's eschatology, the other the Stoa's; translation ran from the Hebrew day-of-judgment TO the Greek philosophical word, not back.

The sitter is האדם — 'the MAN' on the throne of his glory (the ms likely dropped בן before האדם; the packet's transcriber notes the same) — and the Hebrew lacks Greek's 'judging' before the twelve tribes: the twelve thrones simply ARE the twelve tribes', the followers seated over the restored people (cf. the Vat. Ebr. 100 Hebrew Matthew: 'when the Son of Eloah sits in the house of his image... you will sit over those twelve, judging them').

verses.translation: And everyone{H3605} who leaves{H5800} his house{H1004}, and also his sisters{H269} and his father{H1} and his mother{H517} and his wife{H802} and his sons{H1121}, for my name{H8034}, will receive{H6901} the like of them{H3644}, and will inherit{H3423} the kingdom{H4438} of heaven{H8064}.

greek_deviations: Two quiet differences from the Greek. (1) The base text promises יקבל כמותם — 'he will receive THEIR LIKE' — not 'a hundredfold' (mss ABDEFG add מאה, assimilating to the Greek ἑκατονταπλασίονα): the Hebrew promise is replacement in kind, family for family, not multiplication. (2) The inheritance is מלכות שמים — 'the KINGDOM OF HEAVEN' — where Greek has 'eternal life' (ζωὴν αἰώνιον); the Hebrew keeps the chapter's own term (vv. 12, 14, 23, 24).
ירש — 'INHERIT': the land-inheritance verb of Deut (ירש, Deut 1:8), fitting a promise made to those who left their houses and fields.
textual_notes: Howard's apparatus (19:29): יקבל] + מאה ABDEFG; גם אחיותיו] ואחיותיו ABDEFG; ביתו] + ואחיו BDEFG.

verses.translation: Many{H7227} first ones{H7223} will be last{H314}, and many last ones{H314} will be first{H7223}.

one_way_hebrew: ראשונים/אחרונים — the pair of Isa 41:4 and 44:6 ('I am the first and I am the last'); the reversal-saying is coined from the Tanakh's own polarity words.
textual_notes: Howard's apparatus (19:30): ורבים...ראשונים] omit A (haplography).

chapter_notes.summary: Matthew 19 in the Shem Tov Hebrew is a halakhic chapter conducted in halakhic Hebrew. (1) 19:3 asks the divorce question in the court's own terms — is it PERMITTED (מותר) to leave one's wife 'for ANY matter' (בשום עניין, the Hillel-Shammai formula of m. Gittin 9:10) and give her a GET — the rabbinic document the Greek never names. The answer quotes Gen 1:27, Gen 2:24, and Deut 24:1 in their own consonants, names God 'their Maker' (עושיהם, Isa 54:5's marriage-title) and 'the Creator' (הבורא), and diagnoses divorce-permission as לעקשות פה לבבכם — 'the crookedness of the mouth of your heart' (Prov 4:24 turned inward) — where Greek has 'hardness of heart.' (2) 19:12 has TWO classes of eunuchs, not three — the Greek's 'made eunuchs by men' is absent (supplied by ABDEFG) — and the kingdom-eunuchs are defined as those 'who SUBDUE THEIR YETZER' (הכובש את יצרו, m. Avot 4:1's very definition of the strong): continence, not Origen's knife. The born eunuchs 'have not sinned.' (3) 19:17 reads 'MAN is not good; El alone is good' — the christological trap of the Greek ('why do you call me good?') does not exist. The way to life is שמור המצוות; the Decalogue is recited verbatim (the adultery-clause lost to an eye-skip, supplied by D); and the young man asks in m. Avot's idiom 'to ACQUIRE the life of the world to come' (לקנות חיי העה״ב), addressing Yeshua as ר׳ (Rabbi). (4) 19:28 reads 'on the DAY OF JUDGMENT (יום הדין) when the Man sits on the throne of his glory' — Israel's assize-name where Greek Matthew has the Stoic παλιγγενεσία ('regeneration') — and the twelve thrones stand without 'judging.' (5) 19:29 promises 'the like of them' (not 'a hundredfold' — added by ABDEFG) and 'the kingdom of heaven' (not 'eternal life'). (6) 19:24's camel passes through the EYE (עין) of the needle — the Talmud's own idiom (b. Ber. 55b) — and 19:23's 'hard' is כבד, the weight-word that is also Hebrew's wealth-word (Gen 13:2). (7) The chapter's argument is strung on one root, עזב: leave father and mother (v. 5), leave a wife (v. 9), the rich man's leaving (v. 22), the disciples' 'we have left everything' (vv. 27, 29) — visible only in Hebrew. (8) 19:13's disciples מגרשים ('divorce away') the children four verses after the גרושה — a Hebrew-only irony. (9) 19:22 reads that the young man left 'because he did NOT have many landholdings (קרקעות)' — opposite the Greek; ms A assimilates (שהיו). (10) 19:10's disciples answer Gen 2:18 backwards: 'it is NOT GOOD (לא טוב) to take a wife.' Shem Tov's section divisions fall at vv. 1 (Perek 81), 13 (82), and 27 (83).
